items.html:
Contrary to most European licence plates, Italian plates have blue strips on either side of the plate. Furthermore, the front plate is distinctly shorter than most European plates, which in combination with the two strips, makes it unique.

NOTE: Albanian licence plates also have two blue strips, and French licence plates have a smaller strip on the right. However, neither Albanian nor French front plates are short.

Italian bollards are triangular in shape, and white with a black top. They have a red front and a white rear reflector.

NOTE: Albania uses the same bollards.
One of the most common types of Italian road lines are white solid outer lines with no middle line. This is generally less common in other Mediterranean countries.

Italian is the most spoken language in Italy. It uses many double consonants, and typically has a very large number of i’s. You can also find ì, é and à. Most words will end with a vowel.

NOTE: The Italian word for street is ‘via’, and can be found on most street signs.
Italy has a Mediterranean landscape with a lot of agricultural fields on rolling hills, and forested mountain valleys.

Italian architecture mainly consists of pastel coloured stone houses, generally with terracotta roofs. Houses will very commonly have wooden shutters, which will typically be divided in two and open sideways.
Unlike most Mediterranean countries, Italy features a lot of round concrete poles.
Wooden poles in Italy will commonly feature a small white pole sticker.

The most common pole tops in Italy are concrete trident pole tops.

There are several possible configurations of insulators.The two shown in the image are the most common ones.
It is very common to find double guardrails in Italy.

Italian guardrails feature red front reflectors.

NOTE: This is most useful to distinguish Italy from Spain, which uses yellow reflectors. For a good overview of European guardrails, see this infographic.
Italian guardrails commonly end in this distinct shape. The guardrail gets flatter, wider, and it bends away from the road.
It is very common for the back of Italian road signs to be black, or dark grey.
Directional signs are blue with a white arrow. All letters on these signs will be capitalised.

Directional signs in national roads (Strada Statale) are blue with a white and blue border.

Divided highways (Autostrade) have green signs with a white and green border.

Italian kilometre markers are white squares with a roman numeral on top and an arabic numeral on the bottom. The arabic numeral gives you the number of kilometres and the roman numeral gives you the number of hundred metres from the start of the road.

Italian road numbers will normally begin with the letters “SS”, “SR” or “SP”.

The second letter can be used to identify the type of road.

  • "S" when it is a State road, so the number is unique within the country.
  • "R" when it is a Regional road, so the number is unique to the region.
  • "P" when it is a Provincial road, so the number is unique to the province.

Italian chevrons are white arrows on a black background.

NOTE: In Southern Europe, white on black chevrons can also be found in Spain, Greece and Albania.
Street signs are typically white with a thin blue border and black text.
Italian pedestrian signs have five stripes and a basic person without a belt.
These signs, featuring a “no parking”-sign with the text “passo carrabile” are commonly found in urban areas. At the top of these signs you will typically find the municipality (comune) name.

Italy has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.
Italian area codes follow a pattern where the first digit generally increases to the east, then south.
Each Italian region has its own unique flag.
The region of South Tyrol has a German majority, and as such uses German bilingual signs.
French can be seen on signs in the Aosta Valley. Most notably, street signs often use both the Italian word “via” and the French word “rue”.

The Padan Plain (commonly referred to as Po Valley) can typically be recognized by its complete flatness. The plain has some of the worst air quality in Europe, which has led to much of the coverage having a noticeable haze.

The landscape on the southeastern peninsula surrounding Bari has many olive plantations, which are often seen together with bright rock walls. The dirt in the region typically has a noticeably red colour.

Beware that a similar landscape can also be found in southeastern Sicily.
The alpine region in northern Italy has tall, wide mountain ranges and deep valleys.
The Sicilian landscape is characterised by an arid, hilly agricultural landscape, often combined with rocky mountains.

Grey rocks sticking up from the ground are commonly found on Sardinia, particularly in the northeast.

NOTE: A similar phenomenon can be seen on Sicily, however the landscape will typically be much drier than Sardinia.
Cacti in Italy are most common in the south, particularly in Sicily, southern Sardinia and the south of Apulia.
Citrus plantations are primarily found on eastern Sicily and the southern tip of Calabria.
Rice is mainly produced in the western and central parts of Po valley, and less commonly in Sardinia.

A lot of buildings in and around Tuscany are made of irregular unpainted brown-grey bricks.

NOTE: A similar style of architecture can be found in northeastern Spain.
Alpine architecture, which typically features large buildings with white stone walls and wooden details, are found in the Alpine region.

Buildings in Aosta Valley are often built with grey uneven bricks, with an Alpine look.

NOTE: This can look superficially similar to Andorran architecture.
Solid wooden shutters with black metal hinges is a common feature in the northeast of Italy, particularly in Veneto.
Houses in the Apulian region are generally very light coloured, and have flat roofs, typically with two to three floors. The architecture is sometimes reminiscent of the Middle East.
This particular style of roof, called a trullo, is unique to the Itria valley in southeastern Italy. It is particularly common in and around the town of Alberobello.
Close to the Slovenian border you can find Slovene bilingual signs.

The Campione d'Italia exclave in Switzerland can be recognized by its low camera, having a long antenna and a flag. There is also a body of water to the west.

NOTE: This antenna can also be found in several areas in Switzerland.
Etna, the tallest volcano in Europe, can be seen rising above the landscape from far away in eastern Sicily.
The volcano of Vesuvius can often be seen to the south or east from the plains around Naples.
Venice can typically be recognized by its many canals running through most of the city.
Piana del Fùcino is a small plain surrounded by mountains in the middle of Italy with a grid of roads going completely north-to-south.

The island of Pantelleria is a volcanic island southwest of Sicily. Dark volcanic rocks can be seen in the many rock walls of the island, as well as on some houses. It is fairly common to see yellow lichen covering the rocks. The island also has a very large amount of cacti.

The Aeolian islands are a volcanic archipelago north of Sicily. Here you will find a mix of volcanic soil and rocks with mediterranean vegetation, like stone pines or olive trees. Like in Sicily, cacti are fairly common.

In the mountains of the islands it is very common to see touristic white villas.
Within the Aeolian islands, Salina can easily be distinguished from the twin volcanoes forming a valley across the island.

Vulcano is perhaps the most easily recognisable of the Aeolian islands, with its volcano having an almost white stripe of dirt following the top of the mountainside. It can typically be spotted from afar on the island.

The island of Favignana has a distinct topography, with mountains running north to south splitting the island in two.

On both sides of the island you will find flat areas, with many rock walls similar to those found in Bari.

Unlike the other islands near Sicily, Favignana is not volcanic.
The island of San Domino only has overcast Generation 2 coverage, which mostly looks quite gloomy.

steps.title: Maps and resources
steps.html:
GeoGuessr’s own official maps are not very good, for a variety of reasons. Plonk It recommends the following maps instead:

  • A Balanced AI Generated Italy (map link) - 100k+ AI-generated locations.

In addition, here are some resources to help you practise Italy:

  • Plonk It Italy (map link) - This map contains locations for practising each meta in the Plonk It Italy guide from step 2 to 3.

lm.name: Alberobello trullo
lm.note: This particular style of roof, called a trullo, is unique to the Itria valley in southeastern Italy. It is particularly common in and around the town of Alberobello.

lm.name: Vesuvius Napels
lm.note: The volcano of Vesuvius can often be seen to the south or east from the plains around Naples.

lm.name: "Corte"
lm.note: "Corte" means "courtyard". It generally refers to isolated farmhouses or smaller villages. It is most frequent in the area marked although it can appear elsewhere

lm.name: Adige Valley
lm.note: The Adige Valley is a unique area within the Alps, located within Trentino province. Here you’ll find huge amounts of fruit trees (mostly just apple trees but occasionally vineyards too) against an alpine backdrop, making this region very recognisable.

lm.name: Aeolian islands
lm.note:
The Aeolian islands are a volcanic archipelago north of Sicily. Here you will find a mix of volcanic soil and rocks with mediterranean vegetation, like stone pines or olive trees. Like in Sicily, cacti are fairly common.

In the mountains of the islands it is very common to see touristic white villas.

lm.name: Almonds
lm.note: Almond trees are of some use, mostly they blend with areas of heavy olive production, however combinations of almond and olive plantations can be indicative of Northern Puglia rather than the peninsula. Almond trees look similar to olive trees but have more saturated leaves and bloom during the spring.

lm.name: Alpine architecture
lm.note: Alpine architecture, which typically features large buildings with white stone walls and wooden details, are found in the Alpine region.

lm.name: Alpine Landscape
lm.note: The alpine region in northern Italy has tall, wide mountain ranges and deep valleys.

lm.name: Amalfi Coast
lm.note: The Amalfi Coast is a distinctive, south-facing stretch of coastline on the Sorrento Peninsula, west of Salerno. Known for its steep cliffs and photogenic views, a dramatic, cliffy coastline almost always means you’re looking at Amalfi.

lm.name: Aosta Roof
lm.note: In Aosta and valleys south of it, you’ll find roofs made of large, diamond-shaped slabs of slate.

lm.name: Aosta Valley Architecture
lm.note:
Buildings in Aosta Valley are often built with grey uneven bricks, with an Alpine look.

NOTE: This can look superficially similar to Andorran architecture.

lm.name: Apulian Region Architecture
lm.note: Houses in the Apulian region are generally very light coloured, and have flat roofs, typically with two to three floors. The architecture is sometimes reminiscent of the Middle East.

lm.name: Bari Yellow Sticker
lm.note: Plain yellow stickers are commonly found on signbacks in this general region:

lm.name: Barolo Wine Region
lm.note: The Barolo wine region is extremely recognisable as virtually every inch of space is covered by neatly organised vineyards. Once you see it you’ll always be able to recognise it. If you find yourself in such a region I recommend hedging near the city of Alba as Barolo itself is a small village on the edge of this region.

lm.name: Bologna
lm.note: The city of Bologna is famous for its porticoes - covered walkways in place of pavements. These can also be found in most city centres in the area around Bologna, including in nearby cities like Modena and Ferrara, as well as smaller towns.

lm.name: Cacti
lm.note:
Cacti in Italy are most common in the south, particularly in Sicily, southern Sardinia and the south of Apulia.

NOTE: They can be found else where + on some of the small islands

lm.name: Campione d'Italia
lm.note:
The Campione d'Italia exclave in Switzerland can be recognized by its low camera, having a long antenna and a flag. There is also a body of water to the west.

NOTE: This antenna can also be found in several areas in Switzerland.

lm.name: Casali
lm.note:
In the region around the city of Udine the word "Casali" can be found. It basically means "Farmhouses", it often refers to larger farmhouses or is used in streetnames

NOTE: It can appear out of the marked area.

lm.name: Cascina
lm.note: "Cascina" means something like "farmhouse" can be used on top of a road sign, this is a very good indicator for western po valley. It also can be used for village names. NOTE: The word cascina can appear elsewhere.

lm.name: Central Appennini
lm.note: The Apennines run through central Italy, with the highest peaks in the middle, mostly treeless and snow-free. Key parks include Monti Sibillini and Maiella. Roads cross the highlands mainly near Gran Sasso.

lm.name: Cherry Trees
lm.note: Cherry trees in Italy are heavily concentrated around the town of Vignola near Modena. These are very recognisable for their concrete supports if not the droopy-leafed trees themselves.

lm.name: Citrus plantations
lm.note: Citrus plantations are primarily found on eastern Sicily and the southern tip of Calabria.

lm.name: Comune d´ Intelvi
lm.note: Centro Valle Intelvi is a municipalty in the province of Como, located above the city of "Como", on the border to Switzerland. There are 5 villages using the "Intelvi" in their names. Location on the map

lm.name: Dolomites
lm.note: The Alps can be tricky to place, but very jagged peaks usually mean you're in the eastern Italian Alps, especially the Dolomites area. (The Dolomites are a part, not the whole range.)

lm.name: Dolomiti Lucane
lm.note: The Dolomiti Lucane has very unique mountains and rock formations confined to a small area in the southern region of Basilicata.

lm.name: Dry Alps
lm.note: The upper Adige Valley near the tripoint with Switzerland and Austria (as well as connected valleys) is the driest part of the Alps. Here you’ll find very short grass and few trees outside of the mountain slopes.

lm.name: Elba Poles
lm.note: On the island of Elba, poles are uniquely painted a pale yellow colour.

lm.name: Etna
lm.note: Etna, the tallest volcano in Europe, can be seen rising above the landscape from far away in eastern Sicily.

lm.name: Euganei Hills
lm.note: The Euganei Hills are a very good reference point within the flat north, marked clearly on Google Maps just southwest of Padua. The hills are very unique and conical, and can often be seen from quite a distance.

lm.name: Exposed Limestone
lm.note: In much of eastern Basilicata you can find these interesting exposed limestone formations which are highly distinct and localised. (This can be found in the hills of Emilia-Romagna too but in a far more green landscape).

lm.name: Foggia
lm.note: Apart from the Northern Plain, the only other large flat farming area is near Foggia. It is drier, with more fallow land and olive groves. The surrounding hills are low, bare, and often have wind turbines.

lm.name: French Bilingual
lm.note: French can be seen on signs in the Aosta Valley. Most notably, street signs often use both the Italian word “via” and the French word “rue”.

lm.name: German Bilingual Signs
lm.note: The region of South Tyrol has a German majority, and as such uses German bilingual signs.

lm.name: Glass Greenhouses
lm.note: Around Albenga (Liguria) you will find a huge number of glass greenhouses that look very distinct from the plastic ones in other parts of Italy. You can also find these in smaller numbers in some of the valleys further west towards the French border.

lm.name: Gubbio Plain
lm.note: The Gubbio plain in Umbria is one of numerous NW-SE-facing ‘sister’ valleys of the Florence one, and it’s particularly recognisable for the ‘bald’ mountain on the northeast side of it.

lm.name: Hazelnut
lm.note: Italy is the second-largest hazelnut producer after Turkey, with most grown in Lazio and Campania along the central west coast. A hotspot lies just southeast of Viterbo. Hazelnut trees are easy to recognize by their multiple stems growing from a single base.

lm.name: Hillside Olives
lm.note: While olive trees can be found in most of Southern and even Central Italy, in Calabria olive plantations look quite distinct, with these orderly hillside plantations that are often visible from a distance.

lm.name: Historical Area Lomellina
lm.note: Lomellina is a historical area above Alessandria. There are 10 Towns/villages using "Lomello/Lomellina in their names. Locations on the map.

lm.name: Historical Area Polesine
lm.note: Polesine is a historical area southwest of Venice. There are 12 Towns/villages using "Polesine" in their names. Locations on the map

lm.name: Historical Region Brianza
lm.note: Brianza is a historical region above Milan. There are 12 Towns/villages using "Brianza" in their names. Locations on the map

lm.name: Historical Region Cadore
lm.note: Cadore historical region in the region Veneto near the Austrian border. There are 22 villages using "Cadore" in their names. Locations on the map.

lm.name: Historical Region Canavese
lm.note: Canavese is a historical region above Turin. There are 24 Towns/villages using "Canavese" in their names. Locations on the map

lm.name: Island of Favignana
lm.note:
The island of Favignana has a distinct topography, with mountains running north to south splitting the island in two.

On both sides of the island you will find flat areas, with many rock walls similar to those found in Bari.

Unlike the other islands near Sicily, Favignana is not volcanic.

lm.name: Island of Pantelleria
lm.note: The island of Pantelleria is a volcanic island southwest of Sicily. Dark volcanic rocks can be seen in the many rock walls of the island, as well as on some houses. It is fairly common to see yellow lichen covering the rocks. The island also has a very large amount of cacti.

lm.name: Isola di Ponza Architecture
lm.note: The small island of Ponza south of Rome has very unique architecture. Almost all the buildings are boxy with defined outlines along all the edges. Some buildings are also baby blue which is even more unique.

lm.name: Lario (Lago di como)
lm.note: "Lario" is the actual name of Lake Como and some Towns/villages around it use it in their names. Locations on the map.

lm.name: Liguria Architecture
lm.note: Liguiria has a very recognizeable architectural style consisting of larger, more elegant, richly coloured houses, often with painted details.

lm.name: Litoral Romano Landscape
lm.note: The coastal plain south of Rome is very flat and surprisingly warm given how far north it is. A deadflat area with lots of palms, reeds, stone pines, eucalyptus rows and mountains northeast is a guaranteed Litoral Romano.

lm.name: Mountain Grappa
lm.note: Around the mountain Grappa (above Venice) some Towns/villages use "Grappa" in their names. Locations on the map. NOTE: It can be seen on other signs in this area not just townsigns.

lm.name: Nationalpark Cilento
lm.note: Around the Cilento Nationalpark (under napels) on the Cilento coast some Towns/villages use "Cilento" in their names. Locations on the map

lm.name: Nationalpark Gargano
lm.note: Around the Nationalpark Gargano (above Bari) some Towns/villages use "Gargano/Garganico" in their names. Locations on the map. Also you can recognize the park itself by the dense forests of lichen and vine covered trees and the abundance of Aleppo pines.

lm.name: Olive Plantations
lm.note:
The landscape on the southeastern peninsula surrounding Bari has many olive plantations, which are often seen together with bright rock walls. The dirt in the region typically has a noticeably red colour.

Beware that a similar landscape can also be found in southeastern Sicily.

NOTE: Olive trees are common everywhere in Italy.

lm.name: Ossola Valley Roofs
lm.note: In the Ossola Valley, you will find these very unique rocky-looking roofs with small, uneven tiles.

lm.name: Padan Plain
lm.note: The Padan Plain (commonly referred to as Po Valley) can typically be recognized by its complete flatness. The plain has some of the worst air quality in Europe, which has led to much of the coverage having a noticeable haze.

lm.name: Plana del Fùcino
lm.note: Plana del Fùcino is a small plain surrounded by mountains in the middle of Italy with a grid of roads going completely north-to-south.

lm.name: Prato Valley
lm.note: This valley is covered in industrial estates and even more uniquely, vast areas dedicated to growing/storing ornamental plants, something very distinct and unique to this area + Prato is the most Chinese city in Europe and many of the industrial estates around it have Chinese signage.

lm.name: Region Monferrato
lm.note: Monferrato is a region to the east of Turin. There are 24 Towns/villages using "Monferrato" in their names. Locations on the map

lm.name: Region Salento
lm.note: Salento is a geographic region at the southern end of the region of Apulia. Towns/villages in this region sometimes use "Salentino" in their names, which is a good clue for the "heel" of the "Italian boto". Locations on the map.

lm.name: Regionalpark Matese
lm.note: Around the Regionalpark Matese (above Napels) some Towns/villages use "Matese" in their names. Locations on the map.

lm.name: Rice
lm.note: Rice is mainly produced in the western and central parts of Po valley, and less commonly in Sardinia.

lm.name: River Adda
lm.note: The "Adda" is a river in northern Italy that originates from "Lago di Como" and eventually flows into the "Po River". Towns/villages bordering this river often use the word "abba" in their names. Locations on the map. NOTE: It can also be seen on other signs in this region

lm.name: River Adige
lm.note: "Adige" is a river in northern Italy that goes from the Alps, through Bozen, Trento and Verona and eventually ends in the Adriatic sea to the south of Venice. Towns/villages bordering this river often use "all´/sull´/d´Adige" in their names. Locations on the map. Also you can find it on other signs in this region. NOTE: The shortcut a/A for all´Adige can be used.

lm.name: River Brenta
lm.note: Brenta is a river originating from "Lago di Caldonazzo" it flows through "Bassano del grappa" all the way down to the south of Venice. Towns/villages bordering this river often use "in/sul/di Brenta" in their names. Also you can find it on other signs in this region. Locations on the map

lm.name: River Livenza
lm.note: "Livenza" is a river in northern Italy, its source is near Caneva in the province of Pordenone. It flows in direction of Adriatic Sea and eventually enters it near Caorle. Towns/villages bordering this river often use "(di) Livenza" in their names. Locations on the map. NOTE: It can also be on other signs in this region

lm.name: River Oglio
lm.note: "Oglio" is a river in north Italy. After flowing through "Lago d´Iseo" it flows southwestward until it enters Po River. Towns/villages bordering this river often use "sull´/d´Oglio" in their names. Locations on the map

lm.name: River Piave
lm.note: "Piave" is a river in north Italy. Its source is in the northwest of the Friuli Venezia Giulia region near the border to Austria. Towns/villages bordering this river often use "Piave" in their names. Locations on the map

lm.name: River Scrivia
lm.note: "Scrivia" is a river in northern Italy, its source is the Po River and it flows till Scoffera (near Genoa). Towns/villages bordering this river often use "Scrivia" in their names. Locations on the map

lm.name: River Sesia
lm.note: "Sesia" is a river in northern Italy, its sources are the glaciers of Monte Rosa at the border with Switzerland. It flows through the Alpine valley Valsesia. The Sesia flows into the Po River near Casale Monferrato. Towns/villages bordering this river often use "Sesia" in their names. Locations on the map

lm.name: River Tagliamento
lm.note: "Tagliamento" is a river in northern Italy, its source is near Forni di Spora. It flows into the Adriatic Sea southwest from Udine. Towns/villages bordering this river often use "Tagliamento" in their names. Locations on the map

lm.name: River Ticino
lm.note: "Ticino" is a river in northern Italy. After it flows through Lago Maggiore it flows southeastward till it enters Po River. Towns/villages bordering this river often use "Ticino" in their names. Locations on the map

lm.name: Salina Island
lm.note: Within the Aeolian islands, Salina can easily be distinguished from the twin volcanoes forming a valley across the island.

lm.name: Sardinia Cork Oak
lm.note: Cork oak is a good indicator for Sardinia. The tree itself is recognisable when the cork (the bark of the tree) has been harvested, baring its distinctive red trunk.

lm.name: Sardinia Eucalyptus
lm.note: Eucalyptus is a very good clue for Sardinia, where it is far more common than anywhere else in Italy.

lm.name: Sardinia Grey Rocks
lm.note:
Grey rocks sticking up from the ground are commonly found on Sardinia, particularly in the northeast.

NOTE: A similar phenomenon can be seen on Sicily, however the landscape will typically be much drier than Sardinia and it can be seen elsewhere too.

lm.name: Sea of Plastic
lm.note: Italy has a couple ‘seas of plastic’ (similar to the one in southern Spain). Most of these are along the southern coast of Sicily, roughly in these highlighted areas:

lm.name: Sheep
lm.note: Sheep = Sardinia (if not then most likely Tuscany)

lm.name: Sicilia Arid Landscape
lm.note: The western Sicilian landscape is characterised by an arid, hilly agricultural landscape, often combined with rocky mountains.

lm.name: Slovenian Bilingual Signs
lm.note: Close to the Slovenian border you can find Slovene bilingual signs. NOTE: In this area there are also only italian signs.

lm.name: Sunflowers
lm.note: Sunflowers are generally found in a belt stretching from Tuscany to Marche, towards the top of the Italian peninsula, although they are a little more common to the eastern end of that belt.

lm.name: Table-Top Mountains
lm.note: In Northwestern Sardinia you can find many flat-topped mountains with a slight ‘wild west’ feel.

lm.name: Tree Pollarding
lm.note: In Friuli and eastern Veneto, you will find many ‘pollarded’ trees lining the roads. This means trees that have been ornamentally trimmed (similar to ‘Colombian trees’).

lm.name: Tuscany - Landscape
lm.note: The Tuscan landscape is very iconic, consisting of rolling hills with loads of cypress trees. You will also commonly find vineyards, stone pines, and sometimes sunflowers and olives here.

lm.name: Tuscany Architecture
lm.note:
A lot of buildings in and around Tuscany are made of irregular unpainted brown-grey bricks.

NOTE: A similar style of architecture can be found in northeastern Spain.

lm.name: Tuscany Wine Region Arbia
lm.note: Arbia is one of Tuscanys wine-growing regions. These region names are frequently included in town/village names. Locations on the map NOTE: These regionnames can also be found on other signs

lm.name: Tuscany Wine Region Chianti
lm.note: Chianti is one of Tuscanys wine-growing regions. These region names are frequently included in town/village names. Locations on the map. NOTE: These regionnames can also be found on other signs

lm.name: Tuscany Wine Region Orcia
lm.note: Orcia is one of Tuscanys wine-growing regions. These region names are frequently included in town/village names. Locations on the map. NOTE: These regionnames can also be found on other signs

lm.name: Tuscany Wine Region Val d´ Elsa
lm.note: Val d´ Elsa is one of Tuscanys wine-growing regions. These region names are frequently included in town/village names. Locations on the map. NOTE: These regionnames can also be found on other signs

lm.name: Tuscany Wine Region Val di Pesa
lm.note: Val di Pesa is one of Tuscanys wine-growing regions. These region names are frequently included in town/village names. Locations on the map. NOTE: These regionnames can also be found on other signs + shortcut V.P. can be used

lm.name: Tuscany Wine Region Valdarno
lm.note: Valdarno is one of Tuscanys wine-growing regions. These region names are frequently included in town/village names. Locations on the map. NOTE: These regionnames can also be found on other signs

lm.name: Umbria Architecture
lm.note: Umbrian architecture predominantly uses these beige bricks that are fairly distinct. While not unique, seeing them in large numbers can be a good indicator of the region, although this style does also leak substantially into Marche.

lm.name: Valpolicella Wine Region
lm.note: North of Verano you can find the Valpolicella wine region (appears in a few municipality names too), which has these quite distinct terraced vineyards.

lm.name: Veneto Wooden Shutters
lm.note: Solid wooden shutters with black metal hinges is a common feature in the northeast of Italy, particularly in Veneto.

lm.name: Veneto/Friuli Wine
lm.note: Vineyards in a dead-flat region resembling the Po Valley means you are most likely in Veneto/Friuli towards the eastern end of the great North Italian Plain.

lm.name: Venice Canals
lm.note: Venice can typically be recognized by its many canals running through most of the city.

lm.name: Vulcano Piano Island
lm.note: Vulcano is perhaps the most easily recognizable of the Aeolian islands, with its volcano having an almost white stripe of dirt following the top of the mountainside. It can typically be spotted from afar on the island.

lm.name: Italy
lm.note:
Contrary to most European licence plates, Italian plates have blue strips on either side of the plate. Furthermore, the front plate is distinctly shorter than most European plates, which in combination with the two strips, makes it unique.

NOTE: Albanian licence plates also have two blue strips, and French licence plates have a smaller strip on the right. However, neither Albanian nor French front plates are short.

  • In Southern Europe, white on black chevrons can also be found in Spain, Greece and Albania.

  • Furthermore, the front plate is distinctly shorter than most European plates, which in combination with the two strips, makes it unique.

--- NOTE:

lm.note:
• Street signs are typically white with a thin blue border and black text.
  • The name for “Road” or “Way” in Italian is Via.

lm.name: White Pole Sticker
lm.note: • Wooden poles in Italy will commonly feature a small white pole sticker.

lm.name: Bollard
lm.note:
Italian bollards are triangular in shape, and white with a black top. They have a red front and a white rear reflector.

NOTE: Albania uses the same bollards.

lm.name: Bilingual French in Italy
lm.note: French can be seen on signs in the Aosta Valley. Most notably, street signs often use both the Italian word “via” and the French word “rue”.

lm.name: Italian General Tips
lm.note:
In Italian most words end in a vowel. Example exceptions include non, il, per, con, del.

  • Double consonants (tt, zz, cc, ss, bb, pp, ll, gg, etc.) are frequent.
  • Word endings: -zione, -tà, -aggio, -mento (careful spanish and portuguese use this too)
  • Letter sequences: gli, gn, sci.
  • Features of the language include: ì and à

lm.name: Italian Helpful Words
lm.note:
Here are a few words in Italian that can either help you identify the language quickly, be helpful in region guessing, or just help learn the general feel of the language:

  • senso unico - one way
  • di - of (helps distinguish from other romance)
  • castello - castle
  • prezzi - prices
  • piazza - plaza
  • autostrada - highway
  • vietato - prohibited
  • polizia - police
  • sconto - discount

lm.name: Word for street in Italian
lm.note:
Italy typical uses the word "via" on their street signs. Note that "strada" also means street but is the same word in Romanian and used more commonly there.

Here are some similar words:

  • strada - street (used more commonly in rural roads)
  • tangenziale - ring road
  • viale - avenue
  • circonvallezione - ring road

lm.name: Alps
lm.note: The alpine region in northern Italy has tall, wide mountain ranges and deep valleys.

lm.name: Etna
lm.note: Etna, the tallest volcano in Europe, can be seen rising above the landscape from far away in eastern Sicily.

lm.name: Po Valley
lm.note: The Padan Plain (commonly referred to as Po Valley) can typically be recognized by its complete flatness. The plain has some of the worst air quality in Europe, which has led to much of the coverage having a noticeable haze.

lm.name: Salina
lm.note: Within the Aeolian islands, Salina can easily be distinguished from the twin volcanoes forming a valley across the island.

lm.name: Sardinia
lm.note:
Grey rocks sticking up from the ground are commonly found on Sardinia, particularly in the northeast.

NOTE: A similar phenomenon can be seen on Sicily, however the landscape will typically be much drier than Sardinia.

lm.name: Sicily
lm.note: The Sicilian landscape is characterised by an arid, hilly agricultural landscape, often combined with rocky mountains.

lm.name: Vesuvius
lm.note: The volcano of Vesuvius can often be seen to the south or east from the plains around Naples.

lm.name: Vulcano
lm.note: Vulcano is perhaps the most easily recognisable of the Aeolian islands, with its volcano having an almost white stripe of dirt following the top of the mountainside. It can typically be spotted from afar on the island.

lm.name: Alps - Alpine Architecture
lm.note: • Alpine architecture, which typically features large buildings with white stone walls and wooden details, are found in the Alpine region.

lm.name: Apulian - Flat Roofs
lm.note:
• Houses in the Apulian region are generally very light coloured, and have flat roofs, typically with two to three floors.
  • The architecture is sometimes reminiscent of the Middle East.

lm.name: Chevrons
lm.note:
• Italian chevrons are white arrows on a black background.

--- NOTE:

  • In Southern Europe, white on black chevrons can also be found in Spain, Greece and Albania.

lm.name: Aosta Valley - Grey Uneven Bricks
lm.note:
• Buildings in Aosta Valley are often built with grey uneven bricks, with an Alpine look.

--- NOTE:

  • This can look superficially similar to Andorran architecture.

lm.name: General Architecture
lm.note:
• Italian architecture mainly consists of pastel coloured stone houses, generally with terracotta roofs.
  • Houses will very commonly have wooden shutters, which will typically be divided in two and open sideways.

lm.name: Northeast - Solid Wooden Shutters
lm.note: • Solid wooden shutters with black metal hinges is a common feature in the northeast of Italy, particularly in Veneto.

lm.name: Southeast - Trullo Roofs
lm.note:
• This particular style of roof, called a trullo, is unique to the Itria valley in southeastern Italy.
  • It is particularly common in and around the town of Alberobello.

lm.name: Tuscany - Unpainted Bricks
lm.note:
• A lot of buildings in and around Tuscany are made of irregular unpainted brown-grey bricks.

--- NOTE:

  • A similar style of architecture can be found in northeastern Spain.

lm.name: A-Type with orange or red reflectors
lm.note:
Italian guardrails feature orange or red front reflectors. Also, they often are doubled, just like in Ecuador.

NOTE: This is most useful to distinguish Italy from Spain, which uses yellow reflectors. For a good overview of European guardrails, see this infographic.

lm.name: Guardrail ending
lm.note: Italian guardrails commonly end in this distinct shape. The guardrail gets flatter, wider, and it bends away from the road.

lm.name: Italy
lm.note: Italian area codes follow a pattern where the first digit generally increases to the east, then south.

lm.name: License plates
lm.note: A short license plate with a double blue strip on the front and a long plate with a double blue strip on the back is unique to Italy. Similar long plates with a double blue strip can be found in Albania and France, but the front plates won’t be short.

lm.name: Blue-Corners Italy
lm.note: Italy, Romania, Serbia, and Slovenia all look about the same. Thankfully Romania will not have a white/silver border. Italy will have blue corners visible outside the white edge.

lm.name: Bollard
lm.note: Italian bollards are triangular in shape, white with a black top, and feature a red front and a white rear reflector. Albania and San Marino use the same bollards.

lm.name: Italian
lm.note:
Italian is a Romance language and the most spoken language in Italy. Italian does not use any real special letters, only accents on top of vowels: (À, È, É, Ì, Ò, Ó and Ù).

The Italian word for street is via.

Italian is perhaps most often confused with Spanish. Some characteristics of Italian that can help with this distinction are:

  • Extensive use of double consonants
  • Extensive use of the letter i
  • Almost all words ending in a vowel

Take the text in the picture below as an example. In Italian, this text has 5 uses of double vowels, 28 uses of the letter i and 29 words ending in a vowel. The same numbers for the Spanish version are 0, 6 and 6 respectively.

lm.note: Italian guardrails commonly end in this distinct shape. The guardrail gets flatter, wider, and it bends away from the road.(San Marino can have same guardrail ending)

• One of the most common types of Italian road lines are white solid outer lines with no middle line.
  • This is generally less common in other Mediterranean countries.

lm.note:
The most common pole tops in Italy are tridents pole tops with a concrete or metall crossbar.

lm.name: white pole sticker
lm.note: Wooden poles in Italy will commonly feature a small white pole sticker.

lm.name: Bari street sign
lm.note: Bari street signs have this unique logo in the top left.

lm.name: Bologna street sign
lm.note: Bologna street signs are white with blue text and a blue edge, the sign is sometimes supported by 3 small supports (1 on top, 2 on bottom).

lm.name: Florence street signs
lm.note: Florence street signs are supported by 3 small supports (1 on top, 2 on bottom).

lm.name: Milan street sign
lm.note: Milan street signs have a number in the top left.

lm.name: Naples street sign
lm.note: Naples street signs have a unique font with an extra name under the street name.

lm.name: Palermo Mountains
lm.note: Palermo has big mountains in the south and west.

lm.name: Palermo street sign
lm.note: Palermo street signs have 4 dots in each corner.

lm.name: Rome street sign
lm.note: Rome street signs are by far the most distinct street signs in Italy, their bigger than any other street sign in Italy, they have a very thick frame and the Roman numerals in the top right.

lm.name: Turin street sign
lm.note: Turin street signs have this unique font, sometimes they also have the date of the years on the bottom.

lm.name: Venice
lm.note: Venice can typically be recognized by its many canals running through most of the city.
